questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: Units inside a formula
questions.learningObjective: locate a fault by tracing one arithmetic expression
questions.stem: Trace this snippet and state what is displayed. DEFINE netPrice(total, percent): RETURN total - percent. DISPLAY netPrice(10, 2). The shop rule is 8 percent off a 10 coin item. What is displayed, and what does the trace reveal?

options.text: 8 is displayed; the routine subtracts the percent number itself, not the amount it stands for
options.misconception: believes a bare percentage number can be subtracted from a currency amount

options.text: 9.2 is displayed; the routine multiplies the percent by the total before subtracting it
options.misconception: assumes the trace reports the intended price rather than the computed one

options.text: 10 is displayed; subtracting a percent from a whole number always cancels the whole number
options.misconception: believes a percentage subtraction must leave the original amount

options.text: 2 is displayed; the routine returns the discount size rather than the price the customer pays
options.misconception: believes the returned value is the discount rather than the final price

questions.explanation: The rule and the code disagree about units: 8 percent of 10 coins is 0.8 coins, so the price owed should be 9.2, while the routine subtracts the bare number 2 and prints 8. Because 8 is a plausible-looking price, the fault survives testing: nobody compares the output against the rule, they compare it against their sense of it. The tempting answer is B, and it fails because an intended answer is not a traced one, since no line in this routine multiplies percent by total.
questions.hint: Check whether the percent value is ever multiplied by the total anywhere in the routine.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: A step derived from the loop variable
questions.learningObjective: find a loop that skips values by reading its update line
questions.stem: Trace this snippet and state the last number displayed. DEFINE doubled(n): RETURN n * 2. i <- 1. step <- 0. WHILE i <= 3: DISPLAY i. step <- doubled(i). i <- step. A reader expects the loop to visit 1, 2, and 3 in turn. What does the trace show?

options.text: 2 is the last number displayed; the step doubles i, so the value 3 is never visited
options.misconception: believes a loop variable can be doubled and still visit every value in range

options.text: 3 is the last number displayed; the loop walks up one value at a time as expected
options.misconception: believes the loop advances i by one on every pass

options.text: 1 is the only number displayed; the guard fails before a second pass can run
options.misconception: believes the guard stops the loop after its first pass

options.text: 4 is the last number displayed; a value that breaks the guard is still shown first
options.misconception: believes the guard is tested only after the value has been printed

questions.explanation: The loop advances i by assigning a value computed from i itself, so the first pass prints 1 and sets i to 2, the second prints 2 and sets i to 4, and the guard then fails without 3 ever being printed. Printing 2 and stopping is the evidence that the update line, not the guard, is at fault, and reading that one line is cheaper than any amount of test running. The tempting answer is B, which is what a correct increment loop would print, but this snippet never computes i + 1 anywhere.
questions.hint: Write down the value of i at the start of each pass, then follow the update line.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: Clearing a suspect line before editing it
questions.learningObjective: use a trace to rule a suspect line out instead of rewriting it
questions.stem: A report claims the two totals print in the wrong order. Trace this snippet and state the two numbers shown. DEFINE show(v): DISPLAY v. a <- 4. b <- 9. temp <- a. a <- b. b <- temp. show(a). show(b). Does the trace support the report?

options.text: 9 then 4; the temporary preserves the original a, so the swap already behaves correctly
options.misconception: believes a swap without a saved copy would still exchange the two values

options.text: 4 then 9; assignment ties the two names to one value, so the swap undoes itself
options.misconception: believes assignment links two variable names together permanently

options.text: 9 then 9; the final assignment copies the value it just received into b
options.misconception: believes the last assignment duplicates the value instead of moving it

options.text: 0 then 0; the temporary was never given a value, so it wipes out both names
options.misconception: believes an unset temporary overwrites whatever it is assigned to

questions.explanation: A temporary is exactly the mechanism that makes a two-way swap work: temp holds 4, a becomes 9, and b then receives the saved 4, so the pair reads 9 then 4. The tempting answer is B, which treats assignment as though it joined the two names; assignment copies the value present at that moment, so the last line cannot undo the first. Editing this snippet would have changed working code and left the real fault untouched, which is why tracing a suspect before changing it is the cheaper move.
questions.hint: Follow the value of temp through all three assignments, then read a and b.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: A flag cleared inside the loop body
questions.learningObjective: spot an early exit by reading the body against the guard
questions.stem: Trace this snippet and state the value displayed. DEFINE mayRetry(tries): RETURN tries < 3. attempts <- 0. locked <- TRUE. WHILE locked AND mayRetry(attempts): attempts <- attempts + 1. locked <- FALSE. DISPLAY attempts. The rule says retry up to three times. What does the trace show?

options.text: 1 is displayed; the body clears the flag, so the guard fails and only one pass runs
options.misconception: believes a flag cleared inside the body still permits the remaining passes

options.text: 3 is displayed; the loop keeps running until the attempt count reaches the limit
options.misconception: reads the counter bound and ignores the flag in the guard

options.text: 0 is displayed; the guard is already false, so the body never runs at all
options.misconception: believes the first guard test fails because the count starts at zero

options.text: 2 is displayed; the guard is tested once more after the flag is cleared
options.misconception: believes a cleared flag still passes one further guard test

questions.explanation: The guard is a conjunction, and the body sets locked to FALSE on its only pass, so the very next guard test fails on the flag and the loop stops with attempts at 1. The 3 in the guard is a ceiling that is never approached, which is exactly why the tempting answer B is wrong: it reads the counter bound while ignoring a flag the body already cleared. Every line here looks reasonable alone, so the fault is only visible by reading the body against the guard.
questions.hint: After the first pass, write down the value of locked and re-test the guard.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: The operator on an accumulator
questions.learningObjective: detect a replaced accumulator operator by tracing three passes
questions.stem: Trace this snippet and state the value displayed. DEFINE combine(a, b): RETURN a * b. score <- 1. FOR EACH mark IN [2, 3, 4]: score <- combine(score, mark). DISPLAY score. The club means to add its three marks together. What does the trace show?

options.text: 24 is displayed; the loop multiplies the running value, so the marks compound
options.misconception: believes a running total can be built by multiplying each item into it

options.text: 9 is displayed; the loop adds the three marks to the starting value as intended
options.misconception: believes the operator in the body is addition and ignores what it says

options.text: 3 is displayed; the loop keeps only the final mark and discards the rest
options.misconception: believes a running value is overwritten on every pass of the loop

options.text: 1 is displayed; the marks cancel each other and the starting value returns
options.misconception: believes multiplying by a sequence returns the starting value

questions.explanation: Multiplication on a running value compounds instead of accumulating: 1 * 2 = 2, then 2 * 3 = 6, then 6 * 4 = 24. The tempting answer is B, the total the club intended, and it fails for the reason every traced wrong answer fails, namely that it describes code which is not in the snippet, since no line adds anything to score. One wrong operator is worth finding by reading a single line, which is far cheaper than rerunning a suite and hoping a failure appears.
questions.hint: Compute score after each pass: 1 times 2, then that result times 3.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: A parameter overwritten before it is reused
questions.learningObjective: trace a routine that destroys one of its own input values
questions.stem: Trace this snippet and state the value displayed. DEFINE finalPrice(base, off): off <- base * off. RETURN base - off. DISPLAY finalPrice(200, 20). The shop promises 20 percent off a 200 coin coat. What does the trace show?

options.text: -3800 is displayed; the routine overwrites off, then subtracts the overwritten value
options.misconception: believes a parameter keeps its incoming value after being assigned a new one

options.text: 160 is displayed; the routine multiplies the base by the percentage before subtracting
options.misconception: assumes the discount is applied without destroying the passed-in value

options.text: 4000 is displayed; the routine returns the computed discount instead of the final price
options.misconception: believes the returned value is the discount rather than what is owed

options.text: 200 is displayed; the routine subtracts nothing because off was replaced outright
options.misconception: believes overwriting a parameter cancels the subtraction entirely

questions.explanation: A parameter name holds one value at a time, not a spare copy: after off <- base * off the name holds 4000, so the return line computes 200 - 4000 and the price comes out negative. The tempting answer is B, the price the shop promised, and it is wrong because that price requires the original 20 to survive, which this routine throws away one line earlier. The habit worth keeping is that any assignment to a parameter must be checked against every later use of that name.
questions.hint: Write the value of off before and after the first line, then evaluate the return.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: A constant buried in a return expression
questions.learningObjective: explain a one-unit discrepancy by reading the return line
questions.stem: Trace this snippet and state the value displayed. DEFINE tax(amount): RETURN amount * 0.1. DEFINE checkout(items): sum <- 0. FOR EACH price IN items: sum <- sum + tax(price). RETURN sum + 1. DISPLAY checkout([20, 30]). A report says the total is one coin too high. What does the trace show?

options.text: 6 is displayed; a flat 1 is added for shipping, so the extra unit is not a tax error
options.misconception: believes a reported extra unit must always come from the tax calculation

options.text: 5 is displayed; the loop and the tax routine already account for every unit charged
options.misconception: believes the total is only the sum of the tax calls in the loop

options.text: 5.5 is displayed; the flat charge is shared evenly across the two items
options.misconception: believes a constant added at the end is divided among the items

options.text: 51 is displayed; the routine returns the goods subtotal plus the tax it computed
options.misconception: confuses the subtotal of the items with the subtotal of the tax

questions.explanation: The two tax calls yield 2 and 3, the loop adds them to 5, and the return line then adds a flat 1, producing 6. That single extra unit is a shipping constant hiding in the return expression, so a report about the total sends people into the tax routine where nothing is wrong at all. The tempting answer is B, which matches the loop's own total of 5, and it fails because it silently drops the + 1 sitting on the last line.
questions.hint: Compute the loop total first, then apply the final line exactly as written.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: Choosing one discriminating input
questions.learningObjective: pick the single input whose outcome separates two candidate faults
questions.stem: A shop reports that prices are sometimes wrong. Candidate one is a card-type branch that applies the discount only to members. Candidate two is a rounding step that truncates instead of rounding. Which single test tells them which candidate is real?

options.text: Check one non-member item whose exact price is a whole number, and see whether it is wrong
options.misconception: believes a member item with a whole-number price can expose the rounding fault

options.text: Check one member item with a whole-number price, since members take the discount path
options.misconception: believes exercising the discount branch must reveal the rounding fault

options.text: Check the most expensive item in the catalog, because the largest input finds logic faults
options.misconception: believes a bigger input is automatically a more informative probe

options.text: Run the entire price list twice and compare the two output files for a difference
options.misconception: believes rerunning everything is a smaller test than choosing one input

questions.explanation: The useful test is the input whose expected value differs between the two explanations, and a non-member item with a whole-number correct price is wrong under the rounding candidate but right under the card-type candidate, so its outcome decides between them. The tempting answer is B, which exercises only the member path, where a whole-number price is correct under both candidates and therefore rules out neither. Choosing the input that separates the explanations is what makes the test small; size matters because every wasted run costs schedule.
questions.hint: Ask which single item would come out wrong under one candidate and right under the other.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: One change between runs
questions.learningObjective: justify changing a single line between debugging runs
questions.stem: A team applies five edits at once, the fault disappears, and a week later nobody can say which edit mattered. What principle would have preserved the answer?

options.text: Change one thing per run, so any behaviour difference is caused by that one change
options.misconception: believes simultaneous edits still identify which edit removed the fault

options.text: Change as much as possible per run, so fewer total runs are needed overall
options.misconception: believes debugging is measured by the number of runs rather than the answer

options.text: Change one thing per run, so the program stays short enough to read on one screen
options.misconception: believes the purpose of small changes is to keep the source small

options.text: Change one thing per run, so a passing result already proves the fix is correct
options.misconception: believes a single successful run certifies a change as correct

questions.explanation: A behaviour difference can only be attributed to what changed between the two runs, so isolating one edit per run is what turns an observation into evidence about a cause. The tempting answer is B, which trades the number of runs against the number of answers, and it is wrong because five simultaneous edits that together fix a fault leave four of them unaccounted for. The tempting answer is also D, which mistakes a passing run for proof: one run shows the reported case, not every case.
questions.hint: Ask what would be left unexplained if five edits were applied in one step.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: Reading a module result table
questions.learningObjective: point at the module that holds a fault from pass and fail counts
questions.stem: One test set ran against four modules. Import passes 30 of 30, Totals passes 28 of 30, Tax passes 29 of 30, and Display passes 30 of 30. Where should the search start, and why?

options.text: In Totals, which owns the only two failures, so it is the strongest lead available
options.misconception: believes a module with one failure outranks a module with two

options.text: In Import, because it runs first and must be wrong for anything after it to fail
options.misconception: believes the first module in the run order is always the faulty one

options.text: In Display, because the wrong total reaches the user only when it is displayed
options.misconception: believes where a bad value appears last is where it was produced

options.text: In Tax, because a module missing one check is likelier wrong than one missing two
options.misconception: believes a smaller failure count points more strongly at a fault

questions.explanation: Totals is the only module with more than one failure, so it holds the strongest evidence available, and starting there costs the least time if that guess is right. The tempting answer is B, which confuses running order with fault location: Import passes everything, and a module that passes cannot be the source of these failures. The tempting answer is also C, which locates the place a bad value is noticed rather than the place it was made.
questions.hint: Convert each row to a failure count, then rank the modules by failures.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: Halving the suspect lines
questions.learningObjective: count the runs needed to isolate one line by halving
questions.stem: A function has 12 lines and exactly one of them is faulty. The team comments out half the lines, runs the tests, keeps whichever half still misbehaves, and repeats until a single line is left. How many runs does that take?
questions.explanation: Each run halves the suspects: 12 lines become 6, then 3, then 2, then 1, so four runs are needed and the fourth leaves a single line standing. Eleven of the twelve lines are ruled out along the way, which is the entire point of the strategy, and the count is the ceiling of 2 to the power n. A team that instead ran the tests once per line would need twelve runs to learn the same thing, so halving buys the search at the price of one careful assumption: that exactly one line is at fault.
questions.hint: Halve the count each time: 12, then 6, then 3, then 2, then 1.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: A breakpoint instead of a print
questions.learningObjective: explain why a breakpoint gives better evidence than a print
questions.stem: A developer adds DISPLAY lines inside a helper to watch its argument change, and the program starts reporting a different answer. What does that reaction tell you about the prints?

options.text: The prints changed the program's behaviour, so they cannot be trusted as neutral evidence
options.misconception: believes adding output lines never changes what a program does

options.text: The prints slowed the program, so every result after them is numerically wrong
options.misconception: believes slowdown is the only way an added line can change a result

options.text: The prints were too verbose, so the developer should reduce them to one per routine
options.misconception: believes the problem was the amount of output rather than its effect

options.text: The prints worked correctly, so the helper is free of faults and the fault lies elsewhere
options.misconception: believes a changed result means the added lines were informative

questions.explanation: An observation that changes what it observes is not evidence, and a breakpoint can stop and inspect the same state without inserting a line into the program's own work. The tempting answer is B, which fixes the cause as timing; the effect here is on the answer, not the clock, and a paused program has plenty of time. The tempting answer is also D, which reads a behaviour change as confirmation, when it is a warning that the instrumentation itself is suspect.
questions.hint: Ask whether the added line did anything besides read a value.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: Which frame to read first
questions.learningObjective: order the frames of a failure report by where the cause sits
questions.stem: A failure report lists four frames: the menu handler, the total routine, the tax routine, and the printer. Where does the cause of the wrong total most likely sit, and why?

options.text: In the deepest frame that touched the wrong value, because the callers above only carried it
options.misconception: believes the first frame in a report is always where the fault originated

options.text: In the first frame listed, because reports are ordered by the order the calls began
options.misconception: believes call order in a report is a blame order

options.text: In the printer frame, because the wrong value becomes visible only when it is printed
options.misconception: believes the place a value appears is the place it was produced

options.text: In the menu handler, because user input is the most common source of bad totals
options.misconception: believes faults usually enter a program through its interface

questions.explanation: Frames read outward from the call that first received the bad value, and the frames above it are innocent carriers that passed the value along unchanged. The tempting answer is B, which treats report order as blame order, but a report lists the call stack, not a ranking of guilt. The tempting answer is also C, which finds the place the value was displayed, while the printer is merely where the mistake became visible to a person.
questions.hint: Ask which frame first held a value it should not have held.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: Narrowing the input range
questions.learningObjective: shrink a failing case toward a minimal reproduction
questions.stem: A checkout fails on a 400 item order but not on a 3 item order. A team keeps the same program and instead trims the order toward the smallest case that still fails. Why is that a sound move?

options.text: A smaller failing case leaves less that could be responsible, so the search space shrinks
options.misconception: believes shrinking a case adds new evidence about the program

options.text: A smaller case runs faster, so more repetitions fit into the time the team has
options.misconception: believes the only benefit of a smaller case is speed

options.text: A smaller case is easier to read, so reviewers will spot the faulty line themselves
options.misconception: believes readability replaces the need to isolate the fault

options.text: A smaller case is more likely to be a genuine user mistake rather than a fault
options.misconception: believes small orders fail for different reasons than large ones

questions.explanation: Every element left in a failing case is a candidate that has not yet been ruled out, so removing elements one at a time is a way of eliminating suspects without touching the program. The tempting answer is B, which is true but is only about convenience, and it misses the point that speed never narrows the search. The tempting answer is also C, which hopes a human reader will do the isolating; a smaller case is evidence for whoever runs it, not an appeal to a reviewer.
questions.hint: Ask what each remaining element in the case still leaves unexplained.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: Separating three candidate faults
questions.learningObjective: design a test set that eliminates three candidate faults at once
questions.stem: A payroll run reports three wrong figures. Candidate one is a mis-ordered base and bonus, candidate two is a missing guard for a zero-hours week, candidate three is a rounding step applied twice. Which test set separates all three in the fewest runs?

options.text: One bonus-only week, one zero-hours week, and one week with a half-cent rate, then compare each figure
options.misconception: believes a single test must decide between three candidates at once

options.text: One week with all three oddities at once, since a wrong result then names the candidate
options.misconception: believes a result can identify which of three faults acted by itself

options.text: Three weeks that are ordinary except for rounding, since rounding is the newest change
options.misconception: believes the most recently added code is always the faulty code

options.text: The same real payroll week run twice, which shows whether the fault is even reproducible
options.misconception: believes a repeat run can identify which of three candidates is present

questions.explanation: One test per candidate keeps each input clean, so a week with only a bonus wrong, only a zero guard missing, and only a double rounding each point at exactly one explanation, and three runs separate three candidates. The tempting answer is B, which stacks all three oddities and then cannot say which one produced the wrong figure, which is the entire difficulty. The tempting answer is also D, which establishes that the fault exists and says nothing about which of three it is.
questions.hint: Give each candidate its own week that is ordinary in every other respect.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: Counting state changes in a watch log
questions.learningObjective: read a watch log to count how often a value changed
questions.stem: A watch on one variable logged the values 4, then 11, then 14 during a single run of a checkout. How many times did that variable change value?
questions.explanation: A watch entry marks a change of value, not a moment in time, so three logged values mean the variable moved three times, and the first entry counts as a change from its starting value. The count is the length of the log rather than the sum or the final value, which is what makes a watch log a compact record of the program's actual state changes. Reading a log this way often narrows the search immediately, because it shows which update ran and how many times.
questions.hint: Count the logged entries, not their sum or their last value.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: State left behind by an earlier test
questions.learningObjective: explain why a test passes alone and fails in a run
questions.stem: A checkout test passes when run alone but fails when run after a totals test. Both programs use a variable named running that is set to 0 only inside the totals test. What best explains the difference?

options.text: The totals test leaves a value behind that the checkout test then reads instead of its own
options.misconception: believes each test always begins from a completely clean slate

options.text: The checkout test is slower once other tests have run, so it times out and reports a fault
options.misconception: believes test order changes results only through timing

options.text: The totals test overwrites the checkout test's own data files, corrupting the input
options.misconception: believes test programs share storage whenever they share a name

options.text: The running suite reuses one result from the totals test instead of recomputing it
options.misconception: believes a test suite can reuse a stale result to save time

questions.explanation: The two programs share a name for a variable that one of them never initialises on its own path, so a value left over from the earlier test is exactly what the later test reads, and the failure depends on order rather than on the checkout logic. The tempting answer is B, which blames the clock, but the reported wrong figure is a wrong value rather than a timeout. The tempting answer is also C, which invents shared files where the evidence shows a shared variable.
questions.hint: Ask what value the second program finds in a variable it never sets itself.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: Reverting the fix to confirm the cause
questions.learningObjective: use a temporary revert as a test that a fix addressed the cause
questions.stem: A one-line change makes a failing test pass. Before committing, the developer restores the original line and the test fails again. What has that second run established?

options.text: That this one line is what the failing test depends on, so the report and the line agree
options.misconception: believes a passing test alone already proves which line mattered

options.text: That the line is correct, since the behaviour now matches what the reporter wanted
options.misconception: believes agreement with a reporter certifies a change as right

options.text: That the fault lies in the test, since the test reacts to a single line of code
options.misconception: believes a sensitive test is evidence about the test itself

options.text: That the program has no other faults, since one line accounted for this symptom
options.misconception: believes one explained symptom rules out every other fault

questions.explanation: Restoring the line and watching the failure return ties this specific line to this specific symptom, which is the difference between a cause and a coincidence; the developer now knows what to write a test about. The tempting answer is B, which stops at agreement with a report, and a report describes a symptom rather than a cause, so matching one is not the same as being right. The tempting answer is also C, which reverses the inference: a test reacting to the exact line is the test doing its job.
questions.hint: Compare the two runs and ask what changed between them.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: Fixing the reported case instead of the logic
questions.learningObjective: recognise a special case added where a rule was missing
questions.stem: After a coach reports one wrong delivery time, a developer writes an IF that returns the corrected time when the order number matches that one order. Every test now passes. What is wrong with the change?

options.text: It hides the missing rule behind one case, so every other order keeps the same wrong behaviour
options.misconception: believes a passing test proves the rule behind the report is now implemented

options.text: It costs extra memory, because each corrected order needs a new stored time
options.misconception: believes the cost of special cases is mostly storage rather than coverage

options.text: It is too slow, because matching the order number on every request is expensive
options.misconception: believes comparing one number is the dominant cost in this program

options.text: It is fine for now, since the reported case is the one users actually complained about
options.misconception: believes fixing the reported case is equivalent to fixing the fault

questions.explanation: A special case for one order number is a patch on top of a missing rule, so the test suite goes green while every unmentioned order keeps the wrong time, and the green suite now hides the gap instead of closing it. The tempting answer is B, which prices the change in memory and misses what was actually bought, namely the appearance of correctness. The tempting answer is also D, which is the reasoning that produced the patch: a report names one instance, not the rule that produced it.
questions.hint: Ask what the program does for an order number nobody reported.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: Why a one-character change is still a behaviour change
questions.learningObjective: argue that a passing test does not certify a boundary change
questions.stem: A developer changes one character in a range test, and the failing test now passes. Explain, in a short paragraph, why that is not yet evidence that the change was correct.

answer.exemplar: A passing test shows only that the one reported input now gives the wanted result. Changing a comparison also changes the answer for every other input near it, so the edit has widened or narrowed a boundary rather than fixing one case. For example, turning a strict test into an inclusive one also admits the boundary value, which may now be accepted when it should be rejected. The remaining step is to list which other inputs change answer and to add a test for the boundary itself before calling the change correct.

questions.explanation: A good answer names that the evidence covers only the reported input, names that the altered comparison decides other inputs too, and says the next step is to find the inputs whose answer changed and to add a boundary test. Saying merely that more testing is needed is not enough, because the point is which testing and why this one is insufficient. The strongest answer points at the specific class of input a comparison change decides, which is the boundary value.
questions.hint: Ask which other inputs this one character also changes the answer for.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: Repairing the routine rather than each caller
questions.learningObjective: choose where a contract violation should be fixed
questions.stem: A tax routine returns a negative total when given a credit note. One caller checks for it and three callers do not. Where is the smaller and safer fix, and why?

options.text: In the tax routine, so all four callers get the documented behaviour from one change
options.misconception: believes patching each caller separately is the same amount of work as one fix

options.text: In the three callers that lack the check, since the routine is shared with other programs
options.misconception: believes a shared routine must never be changed because other programs use it

options.text: In the caller that already checks, so the existing guard can be widened instead of added
options.misconception: believes the guard belongs in the place that reports rather than produces

options.text: In the caller that passes the credit note, since the caller supplied the bad input
options.misconception: believes the fault always sits with whoever supplied the value

questions.explanation: The routine's contract is what every caller is entitled to assume, so fixing it once gives all four callers the documented result, and the three unguarded callers stop being a permanent hazard. The tempting answer is B, which is a real risk but the wrong trade, because leaving three known call sites wrong is a larger risk than a reviewed change to a shared routine. The tempting answer is also C, which trusts the reporting layer to be the natural home for a correction it did not make.
questions.hint: Ask where the behaviour was promised to be the same for every caller.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: Comparing a fix before and after
questions.learningObjective: read a before and after table to judge what a fix changed
questions.stem: A shipping calculator was measured before and after a fix. Small parcel: 6.40 then 6.40. Heavy parcel: 19.90 then 9.90. Oversized parcel: 31.00 then 21.00. A colleague says the fix is proven. What does the table actually show?

options.text: Two of three cases changed, so the fix is real but its boundary with oversize is unproven
options.misconception: believes one unchanged row means the whole fix had no effect

options.text: All three cases changed, so the fix altered every shipping price the calculator handles
options.misconception: believes the unchanged small-parcel row was also corrected silently

options.text: Only the heavy case changed, so the other two rows must be measured again next quarter
options.misconception: believes a change on two rows leaves the third permanently unmeasured

options.text: The rows show the fix is wrong, because a correct fix would move all three prices equally
options.misconception: believes a correct fix must shift every price by the same amount

questions.explanation: Two rows moving by 10 and one row staying put is evidence of a real change whose boundary sits somewhere the table does not sample, so the honest claim is that the fix helps heavy and oversized cases and leaves small ones alone. The tempting answer is B, which counts the unchanged row as corrected; a row that reads 6.40 twice is a row the fix did not touch. The tempting answer is also D, which expects a uniform shift, but a rule change normally redraws a threshold rather than moving everything equally.
questions.hint: Look for the row that did not change and ask what that implies.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: Keeping the old tests green
questions.learningObjective: judge a fix by the tests that were already passing
questions.stem: A fix makes the reported case pass but turns two previously passing cases into failures. What does the existing test suite contribute that the reported case cannot?

options.text: It records behaviour that other callers depend on, so a new failure is a real cost of the fix
options.misconception: believes other callers of a routine need not care how its behaviour changes

options.text: It proves the developer is a careful programmer, so the failures can be dismissed as noise
options.misconception: believes test results say something about the author rather than the program

options.text: It counts how many lines the fix changed, so a large count explains the failures
options.misconception: believes the size of a change predicts how much it breaks

options.text: It guarantees the fix is correct, since any failure after it must be an old test being wrong
options.misconception: believes a failing old test is always the test's mistake

questions.explanation: A previously passing case is a record of behaviour somebody depends on, so a fix that breaks two of them has traded one correction for two new faults, and the report alone could never have shown that. The tempting answer is B, which is about the author's reputation and not the program's behaviour at all. The tempting answer is also D, which grants the fix unconditional trust; a test that was right yesterday and fails today is evidence against the change until shown otherwise.
questions.hint: Ask who was relying on the behaviour the two passing cases recorded.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: The build that never took the fix
questions.learningObjective: explain why a correct fix appears to have done nothing
questions.stem: A developer edits the source, runs the program from an old packaged copy, and the same fault appears. The edit was correct. What should happen next?

options.text: Rebuild and run the version that contains the edit, since the old copy never had the change
options.misconception: believes the running copy picks up source edits on its own

options.text: Revert the edit, since a change with no effect cannot be the source of the fault
options.misconception: believes a change that changes nothing must be wrong

options.text: Add a second edit, since two edits are more likely to include a working one
options.misconception: believes repeating the change improves the chance of success

options.text: Test the old copy only, since it is the version users actually receive
options.misconception: believes the packaged copy is the more informative object to test

questions.explanation: The symptom came from a copy that never contained the edit, so no conclusion about the fix can be drawn from it, and the honest next step is to build and run the version that has the change. The tempting answer is B, which reads a lack of effect as a lack of cause, and that inference is only safe once the code under test is known to match the source. The tempting answer is also C, which adds noise while the real problem is that the experiment never touched the edit.
questions.hint: Check whether the program being run was built after the edit.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: The first line in a log is rarely the fault
questions.learningObjective: explain why a cascade makes the earliest symptom misleading
questions.stem: A log shows an empty order list at 09:14, a zero total at 09:14, an error dialog at 09:15, and a support ticket at 09:20. Explain why the empty list at 09:14 is the weakest place to start looking.

answer.exemplar: The empty list is the earliest symptom, not the earliest cause, because a later fault can produce it: the load call may have failed or returned nothing, and the empty list is what the program then displayed. A cascade means several log lines are consequences of one earlier event, so the first line is the one most likely to be downstream of everything still unexplained. Start at the last unexplained cause instead, which is the load call itself, and check whether it ran, what it returned, and whether the empty list is being read from stale data.

questions.explanation: A complete answer names that the empty list can be a consequence rather than a cause, names the load call or the stale data as the place to look, and says a cascade makes early symptoms downstream of later events. An answer that merely says look earlier in the log repeats the mistake the item is about. The strongest answers explain why one earlier event can generate all four lines, which is what makes the last unexplained cause the right starting point.
questions.hint: Ask what could have gone wrong earlier that would make that list empty.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: Order of one isolation session
questions.learningObjective: sequence the steps of a focused debugging session
questions.stem: Put these actions in the order a developer performs them while isolating one reported fault.

options.text: Edit the code and ship, because confirmed faults should be closed the same day
options.misconception: closing before isolating inverts the order of the work

options.text: Read the program and predict what it should print for the reported input
options.misconception: predicting after the run gives up the value of predicting

options.text: Run the reported input and record the actual output next to the prediction
options.misconception: recording the output first loses the chance to compare

options.text: Change one line, rerun, and note whether the output changed at all
options.misconception: changing many lines at once destroys the evidence

questions.explanation: Predicting before running turns the first run into evidence, and only a difference between prediction and output says anything; a matching output is itself a finding, since the report may be wrong. The tempting order starts at A, which closes the ticket while the cause is still unknown, and closing early is what makes a fix unreviewable later. Editing many lines at once is the other common inversion, because it destroys the one-run one-change link the session depends on.
questions.hint: Begin with a prediction, not with an edit.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: Two steps that belong in isolating a fault
questions.learningObjective: select the steps that actually narrow a search
questions.stem: A team has one reported fault in a 400 line program. Which TWO actions genuinely narrow where the fault can be? Select exactly two.

options.text: Reduce the failing case to the smallest input that still fails
Rewrite the whole module from scratch in clearer style
options.misconception: believes replacing all the code is a way of eliminating candidates

options.text: Check which module the wrong value first appears in
Reformat every line so the program reads uniformly
options.misconception: believes consistent formatting narrows the set of faults

questions.explanation: A smaller failing case removes candidates without touching the program, and finding the first module holding a wrong value bounds the search from above, so both actions shrink the space of explanations. The tempting answer is B, which replaces the evidence instead of narrowing it, so when the fault survives the rewrite nothing has been learned about where it lives. The tempting answer is also D, which makes the program pleasant to read and no more correct to read, since a fault in logic is invisible at the level of spacing.
questions.hint: Ask which actions leave less unexplained after they are done.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: An assertion that cannot fail
questions.learningObjective: recognise a test that passes without testing anything
questions.stem: A test checks that the returned total is greater than zero, and the reported fault returns a negative total. The test passes on the faulty build. What is the reason?

options.text: The test never runs the faulty input, so it passes without ever seeing the negative total
options.misconception: believes a passing assertion means the reported input was exercised

options.text: The assertion is correct, so the negative total must have come from somewhere else
options.misconception: believes a passing assertion rules out the code path it covers

options.text: The build is stale, so the negative total was never compiled into the test run
options.misconception: believes a passing assertion always means the newest code ran

options.text: The report is wrong, so a negative total is the intended value for this case
options.misconception: believes a fault report outranks the program's own output

questions.explanation: An assertion only covers the inputs it actually runs, so a test that never feeds in the reported case can be true of a build that is wrong in exactly the reported way. The tempting answer is B, which treats a pass as proof, and that is the confusion the item is about, because a pass proves only what was checked. The tempting answer is also C, which blames staleness without evidence, when a far simpler explanation is that the test data never included the failing input.
questions.hint: Ask which input the test actually hands to the program.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: Order of landing a fix
questions.learningObjective: sequence fix, test, and cleanup work
questions.stem: A developer has confirmed the fault and its cause. Put these steps in the order they should be done so the fix stays reviewable.

options.text: Tidy the naming and comments across the whole file while the change is fresh
options.misconception: tidy first buries the real change in a large review

options.text: Save a version that shows the fault, with a note naming the reported case
options.misconception: saving nothing first loses the record of the fault

options.text: Make the single change that addresses the cause and confirm the case now passes
options.misconception: fixing after tidying makes the diff hard to read

options.text: Add a test that fails without the change, and keep it with the fix
options.misconception: adding the test last can leave the case unguarded

questions.explanation: Saving the failing state first means the cause can be demonstrated later, changing one thing proves the cause, adding the test stops the fault returning, and tidying last keeps the reviewable diff small and honest. The tempting order starts at A, which mixes a whole-file cleanup into a bug fix so a reviewer cannot see which line mattered. The other inversion is putting the test last, which is how a corrected case quietly loses its guard when the next change lands.
questions.hint: Start by recording the fault, and keep the real change small and alone.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: Changes that are safe to try while isolating
questions.learningObjective: judge which temporary experiments can be trusted
questions.stem: A team is mid-investigation of one wrong total. Which TWO changes are safe to make while isolating, given that results must stay interpretable? Select exactly two.

options.text: Print one variable at a point where the program is already paused
Replace the whole totals module with a stub that returns a fixed number
options.misconception: believes stubbing a module still leaves results that mean something

options.text: Change one comparison so the branch under suspicion is always taken
Add an early exit that skips every later stage of the program
options.misconception: believes stopping the program early keeps later behaviour evidence intact

questions.explanation: Printing a value that already exists and forcing one branch to be taken both keep the program's logic intact apart from the thing under study, so a change in the output still points at the suspected line; the caveat is that the forced-branch result is evidence about that branch only. The tempting answer is B, which destroys the module the team is investigating, so every later reading describes the stub rather than the program. The tempting answer is also D, which removes the very stages whose values the team needs in order to see where the total first goes wrong.
questions.hint: Ask whether the change can alter the value being studied.
